title: Day-hike essentials checklist
def: The day-hike essentials are the few items that let you get through an unplanned night: navigation, light, sun protection, first aid, a knife, fire, shelter, extra food, extra water, and extra clothes.
look: map and compass as well as a phone
headlamp with spare batteries
an emergency blanket or bivy and a warm layer
use: Pack the same essentials for every hike, even a short one, and leave a trip plan with someone at home.
not: Do not skip the essentials because the trail is short or familiar; most rescues start on day hikes.

title: Deer-hunt day kit
def: A deer-hunt day kit covers the hunt itself, getting an animal out, and getting yourself home: license and tags, orange, a sharp knife, gloves, a drag rope, light, water, and first aid.
look: license, tags, and a pen or zip ties for tagging
hunter orange hat and vest
knife, disposable gloves, and a drag rope
use: Pack it the night before, add a headlamp and spare batteries for the walk out in the dark, and tell someone where you will sit.
not: Do not leave license and tags in the truck, or rely on a phone light to track or walk out.

title: 72-hour bag, car kit, and home outage kit
def: A 72-hour kit holds what each person needs for three days without help: water, food, light, radio, first aid, medicines, warmth, copies of documents, and cash.
look: a gallon of water per person per day
a week of prescription medicines where possible
a battery or hand-crank NOAA weather radio
use: Keep a grab bag by the door, a smaller kit in each car with blankets and a scraper, and a home kit for outages; check food, water, and batteries twice a year.
not: Do not pack only gadgets; water, medicines, and warm layers matter most. Do not store fuel in the living space.

title: Forgot your knife, light, or fire starter
def: When a key item is left behind, safer substitutes and a changed plan beat improvising something risky: a phone light in short bursts, a multi-tool or sharp-edged stone, and turning back before dark.
look: phone battery level
how much daylight is left
whether the trip still makes sense
use: Shorten the trip, start back early, save phone battery for calls and short light, and borrow from a partner.
not: Do not push on into the night without a light or try to make fire with fuel such as gasoline.

title: Clothing layers: wool and synthetics versus cotton
def: Layers let you adjust warmth: a base layer that moves sweat, an insulating layer, and a wind and rain shell; wool and synthetics stay warm when damp, while wet cotton pulls heat away fast.
look: cotton jeans or a cotton hoodie on a cold, wet day
shivering when you stop
sweat-soaked base layer
use: Take layers off before you sweat, put them on before you chill, and carry a dry spare insulating layer and hat in a waterproof bag.
not: Do not wear cotton as your main layer in cold, wet, or windy weather.

title: Headlamp, spare batteries, and red mode
def: A headlamp keeps your hands free; spare batteries or a charged backup, and a dim red mode that protects night vision, make it last the night.
look: batteries tested before the trip
a red or dim setting
cold weather draining batteries
use: Carry a headlamp and spares on every outing, keep batteries warm in cold weather, and use red mode around camp and when reading a map.
not: Do not rely on a phone as your only light.

title: Knife safety and a basic edge
def: Safe knife use means cutting away from your body and others, keeping a blood circle clear around you, and keeping the blade sharp so it does not slip.
look: a clear arm's length around you
a firm grip and a stable work surface
a dull edge that skids instead of biting
use: Cut away from your body, close or sheath the knife when not using it, and sharpen at a steady, shallow angle on a stone or rod.
not: Do not cut toward your hand or leg, catch a falling knife, or pass an open blade edge-first.
call: For a deep cut, press firmly with a clean cloth and get medical care if it gapes or will not stop bleeding.

title: Water filter care
def: Hollow-fiber water filters must be kept from freezing once wet, because ice can crack the fibers without any visible sign and let germs through.
look: a filter used on a cold trip
slower flow over time
the maker's backflush syringe or instructions
use: In freezing weather keep a used filter in an inside pocket and in your sleeping bag at night, and backflush it as the maker directs.
not: Do not trust a filter that may have frozen; boil or disinfect the water instead.

title: First-aid kit contents
also: what to put in a first aid kit
def: A useful first-aid kit matches your trip and training: bandages and gauze, tape, gloves, blister care, pain relievers, personal medicines, and for bleeding, pressure dressings and a commercial tourniquet if you have trained with it.
look: personal medicines and an epinephrine auto-injector if prescribed
gloves and a pressure dressing
tweezers for ticks and splinters
use: Build the kit around what you can use, keep it where you can reach it fast, and replace used and expired items after each trip.
not: Do not carry items you do not know how to use as a substitute for training.

title: Stove and fuel safety
def: Camp stoves and fuel are safe used outdoors in open air, set on a stable surface away from tents and brush, with fuel stored cool and closed.
look: a stable, flat base
no tent fabric, overhanging branches, or dry grass nearby
fuel canisters away from heat and sun
use: Cook outside, light the stove before leaning over it, let it cool before refueling, and pack fuel apart from food.
not: Never cook or heat with a stove inside a tent, vestibule, car, or home; carbon monoxide can kill.
call: Get fresh air and call 911 for headache, dizziness, or confusion near a stove or heater.
